title: Humanoid and Robot-Arm Manipulation in Simulation
tools: Isaac Lab · MuJoCo · PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization) · Behaviour cloning · Grounding DINO · SAM 2 (Segment Anything Model 2) · Gemma 4 · OSU HPC (Oregon State University high-performance computing)
blurb: A simulated Unitree G1 humanoid walks, grasps, carries and places objects; its learned grasp picks up 345 of 360 unseen objects, up from 284.
long: I began in the end of September 2026 with PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization) on toy control tasks, then a simulated SO-101 desktop robot arm in MuJoCo, a physics simulator. I am aiming towards a Unitree G1 humanoid (bipedal robot with Dex3 three fingered hands) navigating to walk around a scene and move differently shaped and sized objects. This is being trained in NVIDIA’s Isaac Lab which can simulate thousands of robots simultaneously on a single GPU (graphics processing unit). This is my first project involving robotics.

Arm, from cameras only. The SO-101 stack has no learned motor policy: two RGB-D (colour plus depth) cameras feed off-the-shelf vision models (Grounding DINO finds the named object, SigLIP 2 picks between look-alikes, SAM 2.1 outlines it). The outline becomes a 3D point cloud, a planner picks the gripper's angle, and IK (inverse kinematics, which solves for the joint angles that put the hand at a target pose) moves the arm. On 200 held-out scenes with two tasks each it placed 369 of 400 simple shapes (92%) and 341 of 400 scanned household objects (85%). A full stack on top, where a language model plans a typed request (“put the toy rhino in the red tray”) and a 9B-parameter decision model picks each skill, completed 62 of 100 held-out requests; the largest share of failures (21 of 38) came from naming objects, not from the arm.

Humanoid grasping. For the G1, we started with a scripted pinch grasp, and compared each learned step against it on the same 360 unseen layouts of six shape classes (boxes, upright and lying cylinders, balls, capsules, eggs). A small policy to modify the parameters of the scripted grasp trained with REINFORCE (a simple policy gradient algorithm) increased the number of objects lifted from 198→282. A closed-loop policy trained with PPO on the Isaac Lab Dexsuite lift task, controlling the waist, right arm, and hand at 20ms intervals, was able to lift and hold 345 out of 360 objects, even when subjected to a shaking test (compared to 284 for the parameter policy on the same layouts, paired test p = 4e-12). What made it trainable was smoothing: low-pass filtering the arm actions, and penalizing acceleration and action deltas. Without these, otherwise identical training runs stalled for thousands of iterations. It is not as effective on household objects it was not trained on (40/342 compared to 58).

Walking, carrying, putting down. For walking I used Isaac Lab’s pretrained locomotion network for the legs. On top of that the G1 walks 1.2 m to the table and lifts via a scripted pinch (26/36 lifted, no falls), and moves objects to another table. For the most recent attempts, 384 robots with six different shapes at their respective sizes walked up, grasped, carried and placed the object down in an upright position while maintaining a standing posture 144 times (38%). For the large boxes, I did a two hand squeeze learned via BC (behaviour cloning, supervised learning from 820 scripted examples) then a scripted set down, the box was placed on the target square 17 out of 20 times during development.

I pre-registered the main comparisons in the project log, and held out the test layouts and chose checkpoints on a separate validation set. The G1 clips are physics from Isaac Lab, re-rendered in MuJoCo. I trained on the OSU (Oregon State University) cluster and AWS (Amazon Web Services) GPUs.
highlights: Learned G1 humanoid grasp: 345/360 held-out objects lifted and held, vs 284 for the previous policy
Camera-only arm pick-and-place: 369/400 simple shapes, 341/400 household objects placed
Walk, grasp, carry, set down upright: 144 of 384 robots across six shapes (development runs)
Two-hand box carry learned by BC (behaviour cloning): 17/20 set down (development runs)
